```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

This package allows the calibration of methylation levels using **MethylCal**, a
Bayesian calibration tool based on INLA
([Rue et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00700.x)).
The package permits the visualisation of the calibration curve derived from
standard controls with known methylation percentages for a selected assay. It
also allows the correction of methylation levels in case and control samples.
If case samples are provided, MethylCal performs a differential methylation test
to detect hyper- and hypo-methylated samples. In addition to MethylCal, the
package includes the calibration and correction provided by two alternative
methods ([Warnecke et al., 1997](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/25.21.4422);
[Moskalev et al., 2011](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkr213)).

This vignette provides a concise description of the package and the code
required to replicate the plots presented in
[Ochoa et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkz325).


## Structure of the package

Two data sets are included in the package:

1. The first contains methylation data on patients potentially affected by the
   Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS). Human genomic control DNA with five
   distinct actual methylation percentages (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%),
   15 healthy control DNA samples, and 18 patient DNA samples are included.
   A full description of the BWS data set can be accessed by typing

        help(BWS_data)

2. The second data set includes eight NF$\kappa$B-related genes in patients
   with celiac disease
   ([Fernandez-Jimenez et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/hmg/ddt520);
   [Fernandez-Jimenez et al., 2012](https://doi.org/10.4161/epi.22846)).
   Human genomic control DNA measured at eight distinct actual methylation
   percentages (0%, 12.5%, 25%, 37.5%, 50%, 62.5%, 87.5%, and 100%), 13
   controls (C), 17 celiac patients at the time of diagnosis (D), and the same
   patients after two years of treatment with a gluten-free diet (T) are
   included. Further information can be obtained from

        help(Celiac_data)

The package also contains two utility functions, `Formatting` and
`TableFormatting`. The former transforms the data into a format suitable for
**MethylCal** analysis, while the latter converts the output obtained from the
calibration and correction functions (see below) into the same data format used
in the uploaded data sets. Further details are presented in

    help(Formatting)
    help(TableFormatting)

Several functions are available for data exploration and analysis:

1. The primary function for data exploration is `ExploratoryPlot`. It
   visualises the methylation levels of the standard control samples. Several
   plots are generated, stratifying the methylation levels with respect to the
   actual methylation percentages (AMP), the CpG position, or both. For
   details, see

        help(ExploratoryPlot)

2. `WarneckeCalibrationPlot` performs calibration of the standard control
   samples using the method presented in
   [Warnecke et al. (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/25.21.4422).
   Similarly to other calibration functions, several plots are generated. In
   particular, to assess the goodness of fit of the estimated calibration
   curve, a scatter plot depicts the corrected methylation levels at each AMP
   for all CpGs within a targeted Differentially Methylated Region
   (DMR)/CpG island/gene. Details are presented in

        help(WarneckeCalibrationPlot)

3. Visualisation of the Moskalev calibration
   ([Moskalev et al., 2011](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkr213)) of the
   standard control experiment is obtained using the function
   `MoskalevCalibrationPlot`. The online help

        help(MoskalevCalibrationPlot)

   also provides instructions on how to plot the results of the two calibration
   tools (extension of the [Warnecke et al. (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/25.21.4422)
   method and cubic polynomial regression) presented in
   [Moskalev et al. (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkr213).

4. MethylCal as presented in [Ochoa et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkz325)
   is implemented in the function `MethylCalCalibrationPlot`. In addition to
   the calibration plots, several goodness-of-fit measures are provided for
   each estimated model, including: mlik (marginal likelihood), DIC (Deviance
   Information Criterion), and RSS (Residual Sum of Squares). The function
   `MethylCalCalibrationOutlierPlot` includes outlier detection, and the models
   are refitted after removing the detected outliers. Plots are presented with
   and without outliers. Further information is available in

        help(MethylCalCalibrationPlot)
        help(MethylCalCalibrationOutlierPlot)

5. The main functions for correcting methylation levels in case and control
   samples are `MoskalevCorrection` and `MethylCalCorrection`. Both functions
   return the corrected methylation levels for the samples analysed. If case
   samples are provided, both functions perform a differential methylation test
   (at a specified confidence level) to detect hyper- and hypo-methylated
   cases. For details, see

        help(MoskalevCorrection)
        help(MethylCalCorrection)


## How to generate the plots presented in Ochoa et al. (2019)

Once the **MethylCal** package is loaded

    library(MethylCal)

the figures presented in [Ochoa et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkz325)
are obtained using the following commands:

1. **Figure 1** A and B are produced by typing

        data(BWS_data)
        AMP = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100)
        data = Formatting(BWS_data, AMP = AMP)
        MoskalevCalibrationPlot(data, Target = "KCNQ1OT1")
        MoskalevCalibrationPlot(data, Target = "H19/IGF2")

   and selecting the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd plot for each targeted DMR.

2. **Figure 2** is generated with

        MethylCalCalibrationOutlierPlot(data, Target = "KCNQ1OT1")
        MethylCalCalibrationOutlierPlot(data, Target = "H19/IGF2")

   Since MethylCal detects two outliers in the targeted DMR H19/IGF2,
   running the analysis for this DMR may take several minutes.

3. To generate **Figure 3** A and B, the case/control samples must first be
   loaded:

        data = Formatting(BWS_data, AMP = AMP, n_Control = 15, n_Case = 18)

   then

        MoskalevCorrection(data, Target = "KCNQ1OT1", n_Control = 15, n_Case = 18)

   Similarly, for **Figure 3** C and D:

        MethylCalCorrection(data, Target = "KCNQ1OT1", n_Control = 15, n_Case = 18)

   For both `MoskalevCorrection` and `MethylCalCorrection`, the list of
   hyper- and hypo-methylated cases detected by the differential methylation
   test (at the specified confidence level) is printed to the console.

4. To generate **Figure 4**, the commands are

        corr_data = MoskalevCorrection(data, Target = "H19/IGF2",
                                       n_Control = 15, n_Case = 18)
        corr_data = MethylCalCorrection(data, Target = "H19/IGF2",
                                        n_Control = 15, n_Case = 18)

   The function output `corr_data` can be used to generate a table of the
   corrected methylation levels for both case and control samples, in the same
   data format as the input data set, using

        output_data = TableFormatting(corr_data, n_Control = 15, n_Case = 18)

5. Finally, for **Figure 5**, the celiac data set must first be loaded,
   specifying the AMP list and formatting the data for the analysis, including
   the number of case and control samples:

        data(Celiac_data)
        AMP = c(0, 12.5, 25, 37.5, 50, 62.5, 87.5, 100)
        data = Formatting(Celiac_data, AMP = AMP, n_Control = 13, n_Case = 34)

   before running the analysis

        MoskalevCalibrationPlot(data, Target = "NFKBIA")
        MoskalevCorrection(data, Target = "NFKBIA", n_Control = 13, n_Case = 34)

   and

        MethylCalCalibrationOutlierPlot(data, Target = "NFKBIA")
        MethylCalCorrection(data, Target = "NFKBIA", n_Control = 13, n_Case = 34)
